title: A Phase 2 Trial of a Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Human Metapneumovirus Combination Virus-Like Particle Vaccine IVX-A12 in Adults ≥60 Years of Age
abstract: Abstract Background Older adults (≥60 years) are susceptible to severe outcomes from infection with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) or human metapneumovirus (hMPV). IVX-A12 is an investigational vaccine that uses virus-like particles (VLPs) to elicit an immune response against RSV and hMPV. Methods This Phase 2 trial (NCT06481579) randomized (1:1) adults ≥60 years of age to receive a single dose of IVX-A12 (150 μg RSV/150 μg hMPV) or the licensed RSV vaccine RSVPreF3 120 μg with AS01E adjuvant. Safety and immunogenicity were evaluated through 180 days post-vaccination. Results Overall, 143 participants received IVX-A12 (n = 71) or RSVPreF3 (n = 72). Solicited adverse reactions were reported through 7 days post-vaccination (IVX-A12, 25 [35.2%]; RSVPreF3, 36 [50.0%]). Unsolicited adverse events (AEs) were collected through Day 29 (IVX-A12, 5 [7.0%]; RSVPreF3, 11 [15.3%]). Serious AEs (IVX-A12, 2 [2.8%]; RSVPreF3, 1 [1.4%]) and medically attended AEs (IVX-A12, 1 [1.4%]; RSVPreF3, 9 [12.5%]) were documented through Day 181. There were no AEs of special interest and AEs leading to study discontinuation. At Day 29, IVX-A12 and RSVPreF3 administration increased RSV A neutralizing antibody (nAb) levels with geometric mean fold rise (GMFR) of 3.4 and 6.5, and RSV B nAb levels with GMFR of 2.9 and 5.4, respectively. IVX-A12, but not RSVPreF3, also increased hMPV A (GMFR 3.0) and hMPV B (GMFR 2.9) nAb levels. Conclusions IVX-A12 and RSVPreF3 were well tolerated and elicited nAb responses against their targeted pathogens. Given the neutralizing antibody response following IVX-A12, further investigation of an RSV-hMPV VLP combination vaccine is warranted.

Methods This Phase 2 trial (NCT06481579) randomized (1:1) adults ≥60 years of age to receive a single dose of IVX-A12 (150 μg RSV/150 μg hMPV) or the licensed RSV vaccine RSVPreF3 120 μg with AS01E adjuvant. Safety and immunogenicity were evaluated through 180 days post-vaccination. Results Overall, 143 participants received IVX-A12 (n = 71) or RSVPreF3 (n = 72). Solicited adverse reactions were reported through 7 days post-vaccination (IVX-A12, 25 [35.2%]; RSVPreF3, 36 [50.0%]). Unsolicited adverse events (AEs) were collected through Day 29 (IVX-A12, 5 [7.0%]; RSVPreF3, 11 [15.3%]). Serious AEs (IVX-A12, 2 [2.8%]; RSVPreF3, 1 [1.4%]) and medically attended AEs (IVX-A12, 1 [1.4%]; RSVPreF3, 9 [12.5%]) were documented through Day 181. There were no AEs of special interest and AEs leading to study discontinuation. At Day 29, IVX-A12 and RSVPreF3 administration increased RSV A neutralizing antibody (nAb) levels with geometric mean fold rise (GMFR) of 3.4 and 6.5, and RSV B nAb levels with GMFR of 2.9 and 5.4, respectively. IVX-A12, but not RSVPreF3, also increased hMPV A (GMFR 3.0) and hMPV B (GMFR 2.9) nAb levels. Conclusions IVX-A12 and RSVPreF3 were well tolerated and elicited nAb responses against their targeted pathogens. Given the neutralizing antibody response following IVX-A12, further investigation of an RSV-hMPV VLP combination vaccine is warranted.
title_original: A Phase 2 Trial of a Respiratory Syncytial Virus and Human Metapneumovirus Combination Virus-Like Particle Vaccine IVX-A12 in Adults ≥60 Years of Age

analysis.summary_en: This Phase 2 trial evaluated the safety and immunogenicity of IVX-A12, a combination vaccine targeting respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), in adults ≥60 years of age. The study compared IVX-A12 with the licensed RSV vaccine RSVPreF3. Both vaccines were well tolerated, with similar rates of solicited adverse reactions but lower rates of unsolicited events with IVX-A12. IVX-A12 elicited neutralizing antibody responses against both RSV and hMPV, while RSVPreF3 only targeted RSV. The results suggest that IVX-A12 may provide broader protection against hMPV, which is relevant for vaccine development and public health strategies in older adults. However, the study's short duration and single-dose regimen limit the confidence in its findings, and further research is needed to assess long-term efficacy and safety.

abstract_zh: 摘要 背景 老年人(≥60岁)感染呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)或人偏肺病毒(hMPV)后易出现严重后果。IVX-A12是一种正在研究中的疫苗,利用病毒样颗粒(VLPs)诱导针对RSV和hMPV的免疫应答。方法 本项II期试验(NCT06481579)将≥60岁的成年人按1:1比例随机分配,接受单剂量IVX-A12(150 μg RSV/150 μg hMPV)或已获批的RSV疫苗RSVPreF3(120 μg,与AS01E佐剂联合使用)。通过接种后180天评估安全性与免疫原性。结果 总共143名参与者接受了IVX-A12(n = 71)或RSVPreF3(n = 72)。接种后7天内报告的预期不良反应发生率分别为:IVX-A12 25例(35.2%),RSVPreF3 36例(50.0%)。非预期不良事件(AEs)在第29天收集,发生率分别为:IVX-A12 5例(7.0%),RSVPreF3 11例(15.3%)。严重不良事件(IVX-A12 2例 [2.8%];RSVPreF3 1例 [1.4%])和需要医疗干预的不良事件(IVX-A12 1例 [1.4%];RSVPreF3 9例 [12.5%])在第181天前均有记录。未发生任何特殊关注的不良事件和导致研究终止的不良事件。在第29天,IVX-A12和RSVPreF3接种均提高了RSV A型中和抗体(nAb)水平,几何均值倍增(GMFR)分别为3.4和6.5;RSV B型nAb水平GMFR分别为2.9和5.4。此外,IVX-A12还提高了hMPV A型(GMFR 3.0)和hMPV B型(GMFR 2.9)nAb水平,而RSVPreF3则没有。结论 IVX-A12和RSVPreF3均耐受良好,并诱导了针对其靶向病原体的中和抗体反应。鉴于IVX-A12诱导的中和抗体反应,有必要进一步研究RSV-hMPV VLP组合疫苗。

title: Diagnostic performance of antigen-based rapid test kits for six respiratory viruses in children: comparison with a multiplex PCR panel and correlation with viral load.
abstract: ABSTRACT Rapid antigen tests are widely used for point-of-care diagnosis of respiratory tract infection (RTI) in children, but how the sensitivity is influenced by viral load has not been comprehensively characterized across multiple pediatric respiratory viruses. In this prospective, paired-specimen study conducted at the pediatric center, two simultaneous nasopharyngeal swabs were obtained from children with RTI. One swab was tested using antigen-based rapid test kits (ImunoAce series, Tauns Laboratories, Inc.) for SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, influenza B, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus (hMPV), and respiratory syncytial virus; the other was tested using the FilmArray Respiratory Panel (bioMérieux). Specimens positive by either method underwent confirmatory quantitative real-time PCR to determine viral load. Sensitivity was stratified by viral load. A total of 1,584 paired specimens from 1,232 children (median age: 3.0 years [IQR: 1.0–6.0]; 53.7% male) were analyzed. Sensitivity of the antigen tests ranged from 20.6% (adenovirus) to 79.7% (hMPV), while specificity exceeded 99% for all six targets and overall agreement ranged from 90.7% to 99.0%. For every virus, antigen test positivity increased steeply with viral load, approaching 90–100% at viral loads ≥10 6 –10 7 copies/100 μL and falling below 50% at loads ≤10 4 –10 5 copies/100 μL. Antigen-based rapid tests for common pediatric respiratory viruses showed high specificity and viral-load-dependent sensitivity, detecting nearly all specimens with high viral load regardless of the target virus. These findings support a role for antigen testing in identifying children with the highest viral burden—who are most likely to have acute infection. IMPORTANCE The sensitivity of rapid antigen tests for respiratory viruses relative to PCR-based testing has been incompletely characterized. This study evaluated antigen tests for six common pediatric respiratory viruses—SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, influenza B, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, and respiratory syncytial virus—against a multiplex PCR reference standard across 1,584 clinical specimens and linked test performance directly to quantitative viral load. We show that antigen test sensitivity is strongly and consistently dependent on viral load, approaching 90–100% at high viral loads with very high specificity across all six targets. These findings clarify the clinical role of rapid antigen testing: it reliably identifies children with the highest viral burden, who are most likely to have acute, symptomatic infection warranting immediate clinical action.

title: The MSC–RSV/HMPV interface: impacts on pulmonary homeostasis, remodeling, and risk of non-atopic asthma and COPD
abstract: Respiratory tract infections continue to represent a major cause of pediatric morbidity and mortality. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) and Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) are highlighted as key etiologic agents of bronchiolitis and pneumonia, particularly in children under two years old. Recurrent infections during the second year of life may be associated with significant histopathological damage and might also be a risk factor for developing chronic pulmonary diseases, such as non-atopic asthma. In adults, these viruses similarly elevate clinical burden on the elderly and individuals with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), causing the exacerbation of respiratory signals and symptoms and, consequently, promoting a chronic inflammatory response that modifies the lung tissue and disease progression. Tissue repair and the homeostasis recovery might be associated with the participation of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs), both lung resident and migratory MSCs, these cells are characterized by their plasticity and immunomodulatory capacity, which are relevant to restoring tissue homeostasis after injury. However, RSV and HMPV may also infect MSCs, raising the question that infected MSCs could lose immunomodulatory efficacy and plasticity, thereby affecting tissue renewal. This review aims to provide an overview of the effect of respiratory viral infections, their implications in the lung tissue damage and the possible participation of MSCs in the recovery of lung homeostasis by tissue repair and immune response modulation.

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on the impact of Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) infection on pulmonary homeostasis, remodeling, and the risk of non-atopic asthma and COPD. It explores the role of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs) in tissue repair and immune response modulation following HMPV infection.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of existing literature, with no explicit mention of systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. It includes general background information on HMPV and its association with respiratory infections, particularly in children and adults.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: There is consensus that HMPV is a significant etiologic agent of respiratory tract infections, especially in children under two years old. Recurrent infections during the second year of life are associated with histopathological damage and may increase the risk of chronic pulmonary diseases like non-atopic asthma. In adults, HMPV exacerbates respiratory symptoms and contributes to chronic inflammation in individuals with COPD.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights the potential for HMPV to infect MSCs, which may affect their immunomodulatory capacity and plasticity, thereby influencing tissue renewal. However, the evidence is limited and does not provide a clear consensus on the mechanisms or outcomes of this interaction. There is a lack of detailed studies on the long-term effects of HMPV on lung tissue and the specific role of MSCs in recovery.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Further research is needed to understand the molecular mechanisms by which HMPV affects MSC function and to explore the potential of MSC-based therapies in mitigating lung damage and chronic disease progression. Clinical studies should focus on the long-term outcomes of HMPV infections and their impact on respiratory health.

analysis.summary_en: This review examines the role of Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) in respiratory tract infections and its potential impact on pulmonary homeostasis, remodeling, and the development of chronic diseases such as non-atopic asthma and COPD. It highlights the involvement of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs) in tissue repair and immune response modulation following HMPV infection. While there is agreement on the clinical burden of HMPV, particularly in children and adults with COPD, the evidence is limited regarding the specific effects of HMPV on MSCs and the long-term consequences of infection. The review suggests that future research should focus on elucidating the mechanisms of MSC interaction with HMPV and the potential for MSC-based interventions in managing respiratory diseases.

elements_en.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative synthesis of existing literature, with no explicit mention of systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. It includes general background information on HMPV and its association with respiratory infections, particularly in children and adults.
elements_en.consensus_and_key_conclusions: There is consensus that HMPV is a significant etiologic agent of respiratory tract infections, especially in children under two years old. Recurrent infections during the second year of life are associated with histopathological damage and may increase the risk of chronic pulmonary diseases like non-atopic asthma. In adults, HMPV exacerbates respiratory symptoms and contributes to chronic inflammation in individuals with COPD.
elements_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights the potential for HMPV to infect MSCs, which may affect their immunomodulatory capacity and plasticity, thereby influencing tissue renewal. However, the evidence is limited and does not provide a clear consensus on the mechanisms or outcomes of this interaction. There is a lack of detailed studies on the long-term effects of HMPV on lung tissue and the specific role of MSCs in recovery.
elements_en.research_and_practice_implications: Further research is needed to understand the molecular mechanisms by which HMPV affects MSC function and to explore the potential of MSC-based therapies in mitigating lung damage and chronic disease progression. Clinical studies should focus on the long-term outcomes of HMPV infections and their impact on respiratory health.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述重点关注 人偏肺病毒 (HMPV) 感染对肺稳态、重塑以及非特应性哮喘和 COPD 风险的影响。它探讨了间充质干细胞 (MSC) 在 HMPV 感染后组织修复和 免疫应答 调节中的作用。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述是对现有文献的叙述性综合,没有明确提及系统搜索方法、数据库或荟萃分析。它包括 HMPV 的一般背景信息及其与呼吸道感染(尤其是儿童和成人)的关系。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 人们一致认为,HMPV 是呼吸道感染的重要病原体,尤其是两岁以下儿童。生命第二年的反复感染与组织病理学损伤有关,并可能增加非特应性哮喘等慢性肺部疾病的风险。在成人中,HMPV 会加剧呼吸道症状,并导致慢性阻塞性肺病患者出现慢性炎症。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该综述强调了 HMPV 感染 MSC 的潜力,这可能会影响其免疫调节能力和可塑性,从而影响组织更新。然而,证据有限,并没有就这种相互作用的机制或结果提供明确的共识。目前缺乏关于 HMPV 对肺组织的长期影响以及 MSC 在恢复中的具体作用的详细研究。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 需要进一步的研究来了解 HMPV 影响 MSC 功能的分子机制,并探索基于 MSC 的疗法在减轻肺损伤和慢性疾病进展方面的潜力。临床研究应重点关注 HMPV 感染的长期结果及其对呼吸系统健康的影响。

title_zh: MSC-RSV/HMPV 界面:对肺稳态、重塑以及非特应性哮喘和 COPD 风险的影响
source_body_en: Respiratory tract infections continue to represent a major cause of pediatric morbidity and mortality. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) and Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) are highlighted as key etiologic agents of bronchiolitis and pneumonia, particularly in children under two years old. Recurrent infections during the second year of life may be associated with significant histopathological damage and might also be a risk factor for developing chronic pulmonary diseases, such as non-atopic asthma. In adults, these viruses similarly elevate clinical burden on the elderly and individuals with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), causing the exacerbation of respiratory signals and symptoms and, consequently, promoting a chronic inflammatory response that modifies the lung tissue and disease progression. Tissue repair and the homeostasis recovery might be associated with the participation of Mesenchymal Stem Cells (MSCs), both lung resident and migratory MSCs, these cells are characterized by their plasticity and immunomodulatory capacity, which are relevant to restoring tissue homeostasis after injury. However, RSV and HMPV may also infect MSCs, raising the question that infected MSCs could lose immunomodulatory efficacy and plasticity, thereby affecting tissue renewal. This review aims to provide an overview of the effect of respiratory viral infections, their implications in the lung tissue damage and the possible participation of MSCs in the recovery of lung homeostasis by tissue repair and immune response modulation.
abstract_zh: 呼吸道感染仍然是儿科发病和 死亡率 的主要原因。呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV) 和 人偏肺病毒 (HMPV) 被认为是细支气管炎和肺炎的关键病原体,特别是在两岁以下的儿童中。生命第二年的反复感染可能与显着的组织病理学损伤有关,也可能是发展为慢性肺部疾病(例如非特应性哮喘)的危险因素。在成人中,这些病毒同样会加重老年人和慢性阻塞性肺疾病(COPD)患者的临床负担,导致呼吸信号和症状加剧,从而促进慢性炎症反应,从而改变肺组织和疾病进展。组织修复和稳态恢复可能与间充质干细胞(MSC)的参与有关,包括肺常驻和迁移的MSC,这些细胞的特点是可塑性和免疫调节能力,与损伤后恢复组织稳态有关。然而,RSV和HMPV也可能感染MSC,这就提出了一个问题:受感染的MSC可能会失去免疫调节功效和可塑性,从而影响组织更新。本综述旨在概述呼吸道病毒感染的影响、其对肺组织损伤的影响以及间充质干细胞通过组织修复和 免疫应答 调节恢复肺稳态的可能参与。

title: Respiratory Pathogens Detected among Pediatric Hospitalizations for Pneumonia: A Multicenter Study from Saitama, Japan.
abstract: Routine in-hospital testing may not detect the full range of respiratory pathogens in children hospitalized with pneumonia. We conducted a prefecture-wide multicenter retrospective cohort study at four hospitals in Saitama, Japan, from July 2023 to March 2024 to describe detected respiratory pathogens and assess the additional findings obtained by multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) beyond routine in-hospital testing. Among 1,170 pediatric hospitalizations for acute respiratory infections (ARIs), 457 (39.1%) were complicated by pneumonia. Human metapneumovirus (hMPV; n=124, 27.1%) and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV; n=85, 18.6%) were the most frequently detected pathogens. Multiplex PCR was performed in 199 hospitalizations. Among 123 hospitalizations in which at least one in-hospital respiratory pathogen test was performed and all results were negative, multiplex PCR detected at least one pathogen in 85 (69.1%). In an exploratory unadjusted comparison excluding 16 group A Streptococcus-positive hospitalizations, antibiotic initiation was associated with older age, higher C-reactive protein levels, and absence of a positive in-hospital test. Among 210 antibiotic-treated hospitalizations without a positive in-hospital test, 110 underwent multiplex PCR and a viral pathogen was detected in 74/110 (67.3%). Multiplex PCR frequently identified pathogens after negative routine testing and broadened the detectable pathogen spectrum beyond targeted in-hospital tests.

title: Emerging Trends in the Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Management of Human Metapneumovirus-Associated Respiratory Infections
abstract: Introduction: Human Metapneumovirus is a significant respiratory pathogen causing infections across all age groups, particularly in young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly. Despite its clinical relevance, there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for Human Metapneumovirus, necessitating further research into therapeutic and preventive strategies. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on Human Metapneumovirus infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates. Results: Studies indicate that Human Metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against Human Metapneumovirus remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. Discussion: HMPV continues to pose a substantial public health burden due to its seasonal outbreaks, clinical similarity to other respiratory viruses, and absence of specific therapies. The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Conclusion: Human Metapneumovirus continues to pose a public health challenge due to the lack of targeted treatments and vaccines. Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.

title_zh: 发病机制、诊断 和 人偏肺病毒 相关呼吸道感染管理的新趋势
source_body_en: Introduction: Human Metapneumovirus is a significant respiratory pathogen causing infections across all age groups, particularly in young children, immunocompromised individuals, and the elderly. Despite its clinical relevance, there are currently no approved vaccines or specific antiviral treatments for Human Metapneumovirus, necessitating further research into therapeutic and preventive strategies. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed journals, clinical trials, and recent studies focusing on Human Metapneumovirus infection. Data were extracted and analyzed to evaluate the effectiveness of antiviral therapies, monoclonal antibodies, immunomodulators, and vaccine candidates. Results: Studies indicate that Human Metapneumovirus primarily targets the respiratory epithelium, triggering immune responses that contribute to both viral clearance and disease pathogenesis. Investigational therapies, including fusion inhibitors and protease inhibitors, show promise but require further validation. Immunomodulatory agents and herbal remedies may offer supportive benefits, but their efficacy against Human Metapneumovirus remains unproven. Advances in vaccine development are ongoing, with several candidates in preclinical and early clinical stages. Discussion: HMPV continues to pose a substantial public health burden due to its seasonal outbreaks, clinical similarity to other respiratory viruses, and absence of specific therapies. The virus evades immune responses via multiple mechanisms, contributing to disease severity, particularly in vulnerable populations. Although supportive care is currently the mainstay, emerging antivirals and vaccines may offer future solutions. Improved diagnostic access, public awareness, and targeted research are essential for controlling HMPV infections. Conclusion: Human Metapneumovirus continues to pose a public health challenge due to the lack of targeted treatments and vaccines. Ongoing research into antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines is critical for effective disease management. Further clinical trials are needed to establish safe and effective therapeutic options.

title: Human Metapneumovirus Nucleoprotein Impairs Stress-Induced Mitophagy and Mitochondrial Quality Control
abstract: Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is an important respiratory pathogen for which specific antiviral therapies are currently unavailable, and the mechanisms by which HMPV regulates host mitochondrial homeostasis remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of HMPV nucleoprotein (N) in mitophagy regulation and mitochondrial quality control, with a focus on its association with selective autophagy-related factors. Using recombinant protein purification, surface plasmon resonance, co-immunoprecipitation, confocal microscopy, mitochondrial-targeted mitophagy reporter analysis, and immunoblotting, we examined the interaction between HMPV N and host autophagy-associated factors and evaluated its effects on mitophagy. We demonstrated that HMPV N interacts with TAX1BP1 and LC3, two key components of the selective autophagy machinery. HMPV N signals were spatially associated with mitochondrial regions, and HMPV N expression increased the spatial association of TAX1BP1-positive structures with mitochondria, while reducing the spatial association of LC3-positive structures with TOM20-positive mitochondria under stress conditions. Consistently, HMPV N expression reduced CCCP-induced mitochondrial delivery to acidic compartments and attenuated TOM20 degradation, while exerting limited effects on basal mitochondrial turnover. These findings identify HMPV N as a viral regulator of stress-induced mitophagy and suggest that its interactions with selective autophagy-associated factors contribute to altered mitochondrial homeostasis during infection.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the role of HMPV nucleoprotein (N) in mitophagy regulation and mitochondrial quality control. The research aims to understand how HMPV affects host mitochondrial homeostasis, a poorly characterized area. Using a range of molecular and cellular techniques, the study demonstrates that HMPV N interacts with TAX1BP1 and LC3, key components of the selective autophagy machinery. title: Maternal RSVpreF Vaccine Effectiveness Against Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Hospitalized Infants.
abstract: IMPORTANCE: In February 2025, Australia introduced maternal vaccination with bivalent respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F protein-based vaccine (RSVpreF) in the National Immunization Program for pregnant individuals from 28 weeks' gestation as the primary, year-round strategy to prevent RSV disease in infants 6 months of age or younger. OBJECTIVE: To estimate effectiveness of RSVpreF vaccination during pregnancy against infant RSV hospitalization in Australia. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective case-control study with a test-negative design was conducted in 9 hospitals across Australia with year-round respiratory testing for acute respiratory illness (ARI) among infants born from 28 weeks' gestation and hospitalized with ARI at 6 months of age or younger, March 1, 2025, through February 28, 2026. Data were analyzed March 2026 through May 2026. EXPOSURE: Maternal RSVpreF vaccination administered from 28 weeks' gestation and 14 days or more before delivery. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Maternal RSVpreF effectiveness was evaluated against hospitalization for RSV lower respiratory tract disease (RSV-LRTD, primary objective), severe RSV-LRTD, and RSV-ARI. Logistic regression with confounder adjustment was used to calculate vaccine effectiveness (VE) as (1 - adjusted odds ratio) × 100%. RESULTS: Of 1012 infants hospitalized with ARI, 655 had LRTD, with 114 of 386 case infants (30%) and 171 of 269 control infants (64%) born to RSVpreF-vaccinated mothers (median [IQR] gestational age at vaccination, 31 weeks [29-33]). Median (IQR) maternal age at delivery was 32 years (29-35). Median (IQR) age of infants hospitalized for LRTD was 52 days (30-89); 495 of 655 (76%) were aged 3 months or younger. VE against RSV-LRTD hospitalization was 77.8% (95% CI, 66.4%-85.3%) among infants from birth through 6 months of age, 80.2% (95% CI, 71.1%-86.5%) among infants from birth through 3 months of age, 86.3% (95% CI, 79.0%-91.1%) among infants from birth through 2 months of age, and 68.2% (95% CI, 42.2%-82.5%) among infants older than 2 months through 4 months of age. Comparable VE among infants aged 6 months or younger was observed for severe RSV-LRTD (80.4%; 95% CI, 54.4%-91.6%) and RSV-ARI (80.8%; 95% CI, 70.4%-87.6%) hospitalization, with similar age-specific trends. VE was consistent across stratifications by gestational age at vaccination, vaccination to delivery time interval, and proximal administration with other vaccines during pregnancy. Descriptively, among all infants hospitalized with ARI, 161 of 499 (32%) born to RSVpreF-unvaccinated mothers had severe LRTD, while 87 of 513 (17%) born to RSVpreF-vaccinated mothers had severe LRTD. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Findings in this case-control study demonstrate high year-round effectiveness of RSVpreF vaccination against RSV-associated hospitalization in infants 6 months of age or younger in the first year following introduction in Australia, with the highest VE observed in the earliest age intervals. Future analyses with larger sample sizes will evaluate VE among additional subgroups.

title: RSV Bivalent Prefusion F Protein Vaccine in Pregnancy and Protection Against RSV-Associated Illness in Infants: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: IMPORTANCE: The respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) bivalent prefusion F protein vaccine (RSVpreF) administered during pregnancy has demonstrated efficacy in protecting infants against early-life RSV disease in the pivotal clinical trial. OBJECTIVE: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize real-world evidence on the effectiveness of RSVpreF in preventing RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) in infants. DATA SOURCES: PubMed, Scopus, and Europe PMC were searched from January 1, 2020, through January 30, 2026. STUDY SELECTION: A total of 1144 studies were initially identified. Eligible were nonrandomized studies reporting the effectiveness of RSVpreF vaccine in pregnancy in the prevention of RSV-associated LRTI in infants. DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: All studies were screened independently by 2 reviewers. Data were extracted on RSV-associated outcomes among infants born to women who received RSVpreF vaccination during pregnancy and infants born to unvaccinated women. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary outcome was RSV-associated LRTI hospitalization. Odds ratios (ORs) were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis with the Hartung-Knapp adjustment and Sidik-Jonkman estimator. Vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated LRTI hospitalization was calculated as (1 - OR) × 100% and assessed in infants from birth to age 3 months and from birth to 6 months, separately. The limited available data precluded meta-analysis of effectiveness against the secondary outcomes of RSV-associated emergency department visits, intensive care unit admissions, and death. RESULTS: A total of 7 studies were included, comprising 7112 infants, of whom 2684 were born to vaccinated mothers. The studies collected data from January 2024 through April 2025 from Argentina, the UK, and the US. Pooled vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated LRTI hospitalization was 82% (95% CI, 81%-82%; 3 studies, 4397 participants; I2 = 0%) in infants from birth to 3 months and 78% (95% CI, 70%-84%; 6 studies, 3008 participants; I2 = 18.7%) in infants from birth to 6 months, when mothers were vaccinated 14 days or more before delivery. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: The results of this systematic review and meta-analysis suggest that postimplementation data support the effectiveness of RSVpreF in pregnancy for the prevention of RSV-associated LRTI hospitalization during the first 6 months of life. The results support the introduction of RSVpreF into routine antenatal immunization programs.

title: Recommendations for the Prevention of Respiratory Syncytial Virus Disease in Infants and Children: Policy Statement.
abstract: This policy statement updates recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) for the use of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunization for the prevention of lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) caused by RSV in infants and children. The AAP recommends RSV immunization for all infants under 8 months of age born during or entering their first RSV season, unless the infant has documented protection from vaccination of their pregnant parent; and for infants and children 8 through 19 months of age who are at high risk of severe RSV disease and entering their second RSV season. A review of evidence supports expanding the high-risk criteria for administration of RSV immunization in infants and children 8 through 19 months of age entering their second RSV season. A discussion of the evidence supporting the AAP recommendations and additional details on infants and children included in the expanded recommendations are in the accompanying technical report (https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2026-079049).

title: RSV Disease Among Hospitalized Children: Second vs. First Year of Life Multicenter Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a leading cause of pediatric hospitalization, yet data on children hospitalized with RSV in their second year of life are limited. OBJECTIVE: To compare clinical characteristics and management practices of children hospitalized with RSV during their second versus first year of life. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter study included children aged 0-23 months hospitalized with RSV infection across 11 medical centers between 2017 and 2021. We compared demographics, outcomes (length of stay [LOS] > 3 days, and pediatric intensive care unit [PICU] admission), and systemic corticosteroid and antibiotic use between the second and first years of life, adjusting for prematurity, comorbidities, and the COVID-19 pandemic. RESULTS: Among 6260 children hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed RSV infection, 1321 (21%) were hospitalized during their second year of life. Compared with first-year admissions, second-year patients had higher rates of prematurity (18.0% vs. 13.4%) and comorbidities (6.3% vs. 2.6%) (both p < 0.001). They more frequently received corticosteroids (53.5% vs. 23.2%) and antibiotics (63.4% vs. 45.9%) (both p < 0.001) and had lower PICU admission rates (4.6% vs. 7.0%; p < 0 0.001) and similar rates of prolonged LOS (35.0% vs. In adjusted analyses, second-year hospitalization was associated with increased corticosteroid use (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 4.28; 95% CI, 3.67-4.99) and antibiotic use (aOR, 2.09; 95% CI, 1.80-2.43), and lower odds of PICU admission (aOR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.40-0.79). CONCLUSIONS: RSV hospitalization in the second year of life carries a significant burden, with higher antibiotic and corticosteroid use despite lower PICU rates and similar LOS. These findings highlight the need for better characterization of this age group to optimize future immunoprophylaxis strategies.

title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine Effectiveness in Medicare Beneficiaries Residing in Nursing Homes.
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Vaccine effectiveness (VE) estimates are needed to determine the effectiveness of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccinations during their first season of availability among populations at high risk for severe RSV. OBJECTIVE: To assess RSV VE against RSV-associated outcomes for nursing home residents. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective cohort study of Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries used electronic medical claims data from September 10, 2023, to March 30, 2024. A cohort was created for each outcome: an RSV-associated hospitalization cohort; an RSV-associated death cohort; a severe RSV-associated outcome cohort; and an RSV-associated thromboembolic event cohort. To be eligible for inclusion in a cohort, a Medicare fee-for-service beneficiary must be aged 65 years or older, reside in a US nursing home during the study period for at least 1 day, have continuous enrollment in Medicare Parts A and B (365 days prior to the index date), and have continuous enrollment in Part D (beginning on June 21, 2023). EXPOSURE: RSV vaccination. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Outcomes were RSV-associated hospitalization, RSV-associated death, severe RSV-associated outcomes (intensive care unit or critical care unit admission, medical ventilator use, or RSV-associated death), and RSV-associated thromboembolic event. RSV diagnoses and outcome definitions were based on claims with relevant International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision codes. RSV vaccine doses were determined from Medicare Part D claims using the National Drug Code Directory. Hazard ratios (HRs) from multivariable Cox proportional hazards models compared the times to first outcomes among RSV vaccinated beneficiaries and unvaccinated beneficiaries. VE was calculated as (1-HR) × 100%. RESULTS: Of 597 430 included Medicare beneficiaries (66% female; median age, 82 [IQR, 75-88] years), RSV VE against RSV-associated hospitalizations was 73% (95% CI, 65%-79%). Among beneficiaries aged 65 to 74 years VE was 60% (95% CI, 35%-76%), 75% (95% CI, 67%-82%) among beneficiaries 75 years or older, 67% (95% CI, 55%-76%) among short-stay residents (<100 cumulative days), and 80% (95% CI, 68%-87%) among long-stay residents (≥100 cumulative days). VE against RSV-associated death was 56% (95% CI, 39%-69%), VE against severe RSV-associated outcomes was 59% (95% CI, 44%-70%), and VE against RSV-associated thromboembolic events was 66% (95% CI, 44%-79%). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this study, in the first season of availability, RSV vaccines were associated with improved RSV-associated outcomes among US Medicare beneficiaries residing in nursing homes.

title: Sociodemographic and Clinical Factors Associated With Nirsevimab Receipt Among Children Aged Younger Than 20 Months in the New Vaccine Surveillance Network in 2023 to 2025.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: We aim to evaluate the association of sociodemographic and clinical factors with nirsevimab receipt among children with medically attended acute respiratory illness (ARI) across multiple seasons and beyond birth hospitalization. PATIENTS AND METHODS: We included nirsevimab-eligible children aged younger than 8 months and 8 to 19 months with ARI enrolled in the New Vaccine Surveillance Network during the 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025 respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) seasons (October 1 to March 31). A mixed-effects logistic regression model was used to evaluate the association between sociodemographic and clinical factors with the likelihood of nirsevimab receipt among enrolled children aged younger than 8 months. title: Recommendations for the Prevention of Respiratory Syncytial Virus Disease in Infants and Children: Technical Report.
abstract: This technical report accompanies the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) policy statement (https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2026-079047) and recommendations for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) immunization during the 2026-2027 RSV season. The rationale is presented for recommending immunization of all infants younger than 8 months born during or entering their first RSV season, unless the infant has documented protection from vaccination of the pregnant parent; and infants and children 8 through 19 months of age who are at high risk of severe RSV disease and entering their second RSV season. The report synthesizes current evidence on RSV epidemiology, disease burden, immunization effectiveness, safety, and cost-effectiveness in pediatric populations; including evidence supporting expansion of high-risk groups for second season administration. Additionally, the report provides an overview of available RSV immunization products, formulations, and coadministration with other immunizations.

title: First- and Second-Year Outcomes After Nirsevimab Immunization.
abstract: IMPORTANCE: The consistency of nirsevimab effectiveness across consecutive seasons and its broader clinical protective effects remain to be fully characterized. OBJECTIVE: To assess whether first-season effectiveness of nirsevimab against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)-lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI)-related hospitalizations is maintained during a new RSV season, whether the effectiveness persists beyond the first season, and whether nirsevimab exposure is associated with hospitalizations for non-RSV infections and asthma during the first and second years of follow-up. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This cohort study analyzed 2 nationwide matched cohorts using the French National Health Data System, including infants born in metropolitan France before the 2023 and 2024 immunization campaigns. Infants receiving nirsevimab were matched 1:1 to unimmunized infants. Both cohorts were followed up for 1 year after immunization, with an additional second year of follow-up for the 2023 cohort. Data analysis was performed from February 2023 to August 2025. EXPOSURES: Single dose of nirsevimab. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: RSV-LRTI-related, non-RSV infection, and asthma hospitalizations were assessed using weighted Cox proportional hazards models. RESULTS: This cohort study included 74 672 infants in 2023 and 175 526 in 2024. At baseline, the mean (SD) age of immunized infants was 4.5 (2.0) months in the 2023 cohort; 19 633 (52.6%) were male and 17 703 (47.4%) were female. The mean (SD) age of the 2024 cohort was 4.8 (2.2) months; 44 863 immunized infants (51.1%) were male and 42 900 (48.9%) were female. Among 37 366 infant pairs in 2023 and 87 763 pairs in 2024, RSV-LRTI-related hospitalizations during the first year of follow-up occurred in 299 (0.8%) immunized vs 899 (2.4%) unimmunized infants in 2023 and 456 (0.5%) vs 1711 (1.9%), respectively, in 2024. Nirsevimab was associated with a lower rate of RSV-LRTI-related hospitalization in both the 2023 and 2024 cohort during the first year of follow-up, with effectiveness estimates of 66% (95% CI, 61%-70%) and 72% (95% CI, 69%-75%), respectively. An association with higher rates of hospitalization for ear, nose, and throat (ENT) bacterial infections was observed (2023 cohort: weighted hazard ratio [wHR], 1.36; 95% CI, 1.00-1.84; 2024 cohort: wHR, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.15-1.78). No significant association was observed for other outcomes. During the second year of follow-up, no protective association was observed for RSV-LRTI-related hospitalization (wHR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.73-1.43). An association with higher rates of hospitalization for ENT (wHR, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.10-2.22) and asthma (wHR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.05-1.46) was observed. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: This study found that nirsevimab was associated with a substantial reduction in RSV-LRTI-related hospitalizations during the first year across both the 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 seasons. It was not associated with reduced hospitalizations due to non-RSV infections or asthma, nor during the second year of follow-up.

title: Upper Airway and Neurological Manifestations of Pediatric Omicron Infection: From Novel Pathogen to Endemic Respiratory Virus — A Natural Experiment in Immuno-naive versus Primed Children
abstract: Abstract Background The Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2 has been associated with altered clinical phenotypes in children, including upper airway involvement and neurological complications. However, the magnitude of these manifestations relative to established pediatric respiratory viruses remains incompletely quantified, and the extent to which immune priming attenuates severity is unknown. We aimed to characterize upper airway obstruction (UAO) and neurological events in hospitalized children with Omicron infection, to compare outcomes with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human rhinovirus (HRV) using propensity score-matched analyzes, and to leverage a unique natural experiment to assess the impact of first versus second immune exposure on disease severity. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, we identified 2,085 hospitalized children (0–18 years) with laboratory-confirmed infection: 211 with Omicron (temporal proxy), 424 with RSV, 824 with HRV, and 957 with other viruses. Primary outcomes were UAO and neurological events. Propensity score matching (1:2) compared Omicron with RSV and HRV, adjusting for age, sex, comorbidities, and admission severity. A natural-experiment analysis compared first exposure (Wave 1, December 2022–February 2023, n = 82) versus second exposure (Wave 2+, March–December 2023, n = 51) among children ≥ 6 months of age. Age-stratified and wave-period analyzes were prespecified. Results UAO occurred in 20 of 211 children with Omicron (9.5%, 95% CI 5.9–14.2%) versus 1 of 424 with RSV (0.2%) and 1 of 824 with HRV (0.2%). Any neurological event was observed in 44 of 211 with Omicron (20.9%, 95% CI 15.7–26.9%) versus 20 of 424 with RSV (4.7%) and 26 of 824 with HRV (3.2%). After matching, Omicron was associated with increased risks of MODS score ≥ 2 (vs. RSV: RR 3.80, 95% CI 1.84–7.86; vs. HRV: RR 4.50, 95% CI 2.32–8.72), non-febrile neurological events (vs. RSV: RR 5.2, 95% CI 2.8–9.6; vs. HRV: RR 6.8, 95% CI 3.9–11.8), and severe adverse outcomes (vs. RSV: RR 3.08, 95% CI 1.52–6.24; vs. HRV: RR 3.85, 95% CI 1.98–7.49). In the immune exposure analysis, severe outcomes were markedly lower after second exposure (13.7%) than after first exposure (45.1%; p < 0.001), representing a 71% relative reduction. UAO decreased from 18.3% to 2.0% (p = 0.005), while LRTI rates were unchanged (45.1% vs. 56.9%; p = 0.214), indicating immune “taming” of severity without prevention of infection. Conclusions Pediatric Omicron infection was associated with substantially higher rates of UAO and neurological events than RSV or HRV, with risks extending beyond infancy. Immune priming dramatically attenuated severe outcomes and upper airway toxicity, though lower respiratory involvement persisted. These findings document the transition of Omicron from a novel, severe pediatric pathogen toward an established respiratory virus, and highlight the need for age-specific clinical vigilance and ongoing surveillance.

After matching, Omicron was associated with increased risks of MODS score ≥ 2 (vs. RSV: RR 3.80, 95% CI 1.84–7.86; vs. HRV: RR 4.50, 95% CI 2.32–8.72), non-febrile neurological events (vs. RSV: RR 5.2, 95% CI 2.8–9.6; vs. HRV: RR 6.8, 95% CI 3.9–11.8), and severe adverse outcomes (vs. RSV: RR 3.08, 95% CI 1.52–6.24; vs. HRV: RR 3.85, 95% CI 1.98–7.49). These findings document the transition of Omicron from a novel, severe pediatric pathogen toward an established respiratory virus, and highlight the need for age-specific clinical vigilance and ongoing surveillance.

source_records.abstract: Abstract Background The Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2 has been associated with altered clinical phenotypes in children, including upper airway involvement and neurological complications. However, the magnitude of these manifestations relative to established pediatric respiratory viruses remains incompletely quantified, and the extent to which immune priming attenuates severity is unknown. We aimed to characterize upper airway obstruction (UAO) and neurological events in hospitalized children with Omicron infection, to compare outcomes with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and human rhinovirus (HRV) using propensity score-matched analyzes, and to leverage a unique natural experiment to assess the impact of first versus second immune exposure on disease severity. Methods In this retrospective cohort study, we identified 2,085 hospitalized children (0–18 years) with laboratory-confirmed infection: 211 with Omicron (temporal proxy), 424 with RSV, 824 with HRV, and 957 with other viruses. Primary outcomes were UAO and neurological events. Propensity score matching (1:2) compared Omicron with RSV and HRV, adjusting for age, sex, comorbidities, and admission severity. A natural-experiment analysis compared first exposure (Wave 1, December 2022–February 2023, n = 82) versus second exposure (Wave 2+, March–December 2023, n = 51) among children ≥ 6 months of age. Age-stratified and wave-period analyzes were prespecified. Results UAO occurred in 20 of 211 children with Omicron (9.5%, 95% CI 5.9–14.2%) versus 1 of 424 with RSV (0.2%) and 1 of 824 with HRV (0.2%). Any neurological event was observed in 44 of 211 with Omicron (20.9%, 95% CI 15.7–26.9%) versus 20 of 424 with RSV (4.7%) and 26 of 824 with HRV (3.2%). After matching, Omicron was associated with increased risks of MODS score ≥ 2 (vs. RSV: RR 3.80, 95% CI 1.84–7.86; vs. HRV: RR 4.50, 95% CI 2.32–8.72), non-febrile neurological events (vs. RSV: RR 5.2, 95% CI 2.8–9.6; vs. HRV: RR 6.8, 95% CI 3.9–11.8), and severe adverse outcomes (vs. RSV: RR 3.08, 95% CI 1.52–6.24; vs. HRV: RR 3.85, 95% CI 1.98–7.49). In the immune exposure analysis, severe outcomes were markedly lower after second exposure (13.7%) than after first exposure (45.1%; p < 0.001), representing a 71% relative reduction. UAO decreased from 18.3% to 2.0% (p = 0.005), while LRTI rates were unchanged (45.1% vs. 56.9%; p = 0.214), indicating immune “taming” of severity without prevention of infection. Conclusions Pediatric Omicron infection was associated with substantially higher rates of UAO and neurological events than RSV or HRV, with risks extending beyond infancy. Immune priming dramatically attenuated severe outcomes and upper airway toxicity, though lower respiratory involvement persisted. These findings document the transition of Omicron from a novel, severe pediatric pathogen toward an established respiratory virus, and highlight the need for age-specific clinical vigilance and ongoing surveillance.

title: Human type 3 parainfluenza virus activates NK cells after in vitro stimulation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells
abstract: Parainfluenza virus (PIV), along with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), metapneumoviruses, influenza A and B viruses, adenoviruses, etc. plays a significant role in prevalence of acute respiratory viral infections, causing inflammation of upper and lower respiratory tract which may lead to severe bronchitis and pneumonia, especially in young children and immunocompromised adults. Moreover, parainfluenza infection frequently complicates chronic diseases such as asthma and COPD. However, there is currently no specific prophylaxis against parainfluenza, although vaccine development is actively underway worldwide. Smorodintsev Department of Virology and Immunology at the Institute of Experimental Medicine is developing a domestic T cell vaccine against RSV, metapneumovirus, and human PIV type 3 (PIV3). This vaccine is based on a live attenuated influenza vaccine vector. The study revealed high IFNγ expression in cells with the CD3- phenotype. Eleven healthy volunteers aged 23 to 43 years participated in this trial. Their peripheral blood mononuclear cells were stimulated with H1N1, H3N2, RSV, and PIV3 influenza viruses using a panel of antibodies against CD3, CD8, CD4, CD197, CD45RA, CD56, IFNγ, and TNFα antigens. The study was conducted by means of multicolor flow cytometry. It was found that natural killer cells with the CD3-CD56+ phenotype synthesize significant amounts of interferon-γ when treated by human PIV3, but they do not respond to stimulation by RSV and H1N1 and H3N2 influenza viruses. Furthermore, it was found that NK cells release TNFα when stimulated by PIV3, but they are not polyfunctional. The results of this study are consistent with research published worldwide, and they suggest a unique mechanism of immune response to PIV3, which can be used in development of T cell vaccines against human PIV.

full_text: SummaryCoinfections may influence the clinical outcome of respiratory illness. Data are limited regarding RSV coinfections in adults with high‐risk conditions. Residual respiratory specimens from community‐dwelling adults (≥ 18 years) with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition were retested using a multiplex panel for multiple viral pathogens. We compared demographic and clinical characteristics between those with RSV coinfection versus RSV single infection. RSV coinfections comprised 5.9% of all RSV infections among adults with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition. No statistically significant differences were observed between those with RSV coinfections and single infections according to presence of specific high‐risk conditions or clinical disease presentation.Keywords: adults, coinfections, high‐risk conditions, respiratory syncytial virus 2.MethodsThis retrospective cohort study used existing data and archived respiratory specimens from community‐dwelling adult participants who were originally enrolled in test‐negative studies of influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) during 2015–2020 winter seasons. The details of these VE studies have been described in detail elsewhere [4] and are summarized briefly below.2.1.Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness StudyOriginal VE studies enrolled Marshfield Clinic Health System (MCHS) patients in Marshfield, WI, concordant with an outpatient clinic encounter for an acute respiratory illness (ARI), during winter seasons (January 2016–April 2016, January 2017–April 2017, December 2017–April 2018, January 2019–April 2019, December 2019–March 2020). Eligible participants had illness duration of ≤ 7 days at the time of enrollment. Individuals with enrollment in the past 14 days or receipt of an antiviral drug before sample collection were ineligible. Participants provided respiratory samples (nasal and throat) for influenza testing. Residual samples were subsequently archived.2.2.Current StudyThe current analysis included VE study participants aged ≥ 18 years with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition. Archived respiratory samples were retested on a multiplex panel (GenMark ePlex Respiratory Pathogen Panel) [5] for adenovirus (AdV), seasonal coronaviruses (CoV; types 229E, HKU1, NL63, OC43), human metapneumovirus (hMPV), rhinovirus/enterovirus (RV), influenza virus (IFV; A/H1, A/H1pdm09, H3, B), parainfluenza virus (PIV; types 1–4), and RSV (types A, B). RSV coinfection was defined as detection of ≥ 2 viral pathogens, one of which was RSV A or B and the other non‐RSV. Infection with RSV A and B simultaneously, without the presence of a non‐RSV pathogen, was not considered a coinfection. High‐risk conditions were defined using International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes documented in the electronic health record (EHR) (Appendix A). Conditions were grouped into cardiac disorders, chronic respiratory diseases, chronic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and immunocompromised status. Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) score at time of VE study enrollment, and hospitalization within 30 days of enrollment visit, were also obtained from the EHR.2.3.Ethics StatementThe MCHS institutional review board reviewed and approved this study with a waiver of informed consent. Patients provided consent before participating in the original Flu VE study. 4.ResultsOf 3601 samples retested from eligible enrollments of high‐risk adults, RSV was detected in 303 (8.4%). Prevalence of RSV coinfections varied by age, and occurred with RV (n = 8; 44.4%); IFV (n = 6; 33.3%); CoV (n = 5; 27.8%); and AdV (n = 1; 5.6%) (Figure 1). AdV, adenovirus; CoV, coronaviruses (seasonal); EV, enterovirus; HMpV, human metapneumovirus; IFV, influenza virus; PIV, parainfluenza virus; RSV, respiratory syncytial virus. RV, rhinovirusIn the 30 days after enrollment, there were 0 hospitalizations among RSV coinfections and 8 hospitalizations (2.6%) among RSV single infections. During this period, RSV‐coinfected individuals experienced 2 (11.1%), 1 (5.6%) and 1 (5.6%) cases of asthma exacerbation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation, and pneumonia, respectively. Among RSV single infections, there were 10 (3.5%), 19 (6.7%) and 13 (4.6%) cases with asthma exacerbation, COPD exacerbation, and pneumonia, respectively. There were no statistically significant differences between those with RSV coinfections versus single infections by age group, sex, vaccination status, presence of upper or lower respiratory symptoms, or high‐risk conditions. 5.DiscussionIn this retrospective cohort study of high‐risk adults, RSV coinfections comprised 5.9% of all RSV outpatient ARI. The relatively low proportion of RSV coinfections observed among high‐risk adults in our study is consistent with previous studies of hospitalized children and adults, where respiratory viral coinfections (including coinfections with RSV) varied from 5.0% to 14.4%, and were inversely associated with age [6, 7]. full_text_sections.abstract: SummaryCoinfections may influence the clinical outcome of respiratory illness. Data are limited regarding RSV coinfections in adults with high‐risk conditions. Residual respiratory specimens from community‐dwelling adults (≥ 18 years) with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition were retested using a multiplex panel for multiple viral pathogens. We compared demographic and clinical characteristics between those with RSV coinfection versus RSV single infection. RSV coinfections comprised 5.9% of all RSV infections among adults with ≥ 1 high‐risk condition. No statistically significant differences were observed between those with RSV coinfections and single infections according to presence of specific high‐risk conditions or clinical disease presentation.Keywords: adults, coinfections, high‐risk conditions, respiratory syncytial virus

title_original: Coinfections With Respiratory Syncytial Virus in a Cohort of Adults With High‐Risk Conditions, 2015–2020: A Retrospective Observational Study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate RSV coinfections in high-risk adults, addressing a knowledge gap regarding the significance of RSV coinfections in this population, which may be at increased risk for severe infection.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A retrospective observational study of 3601 respiratory samples from adults with high-risk conditions over five winter seasons from 2015 to 2020, focusing on RSV coinfections.
analysis.methods: Residual respiratory specimens from community-dwelling adults with ≥1 high-risk conditions were retested using a multiplex panel for multiple viral pathogens, with RSV coinfection defined as detection of ≥2 viral pathogens, one of which was RSV A or B and the other non-RSV.
analysis.main_results: RSV was detected in 303 (8.4%) of 3601 samples, with 5.9% of RSV-positive adults having coinfections, primarily with rhinovirus (RV) and influenza virus (IFV).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that RSV coinfections were most common with RV and IFV, and there were no statistically significant differences between coinfections and single infections according to high-risk conditions, potentially due to limited statistical power.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that RSV coinfections may be associated with increased disease severity in high-risk adults, highlighting the need for further research and surveillance in this population.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study had a relatively small sample size and low number of RSV coinfections detected, limiting the ability to detect differences between coinfections and single infections. The study period was before the COVID-19 pandemic and did not include coinfections with SARS-CoV-2.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated RSV coinfections in high-risk adults, finding that 5.9% of RSV-positive adults had coinfections, primarily with rhinovirus and influenza virus. The findings suggest a need for further research and surveillance in this population.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查高危成人中 RSV 合并感染的情况,解决该人群中 RSV 合并感染重要性的知识差距,因为该人群严重感染的风险可能会增加。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 对 2015 年至 2020 年五个冬季的 3601 份高危成年人呼吸道样本进行回顾性观察研究,重点关注 RSV 合并感染。
elements_zh.methods: 使用多重检测组对患有 ≥1 种高危病症的社区居住成年人的残留呼吸道标本进行了多种病毒病原体的重新检测,RSV 合并感染定义为检测到 ≥2 种病毒病原体,其中一种是 RSV A 或 B,另一种是非 RSV。
elements_zh.main_results: 3601 份样本中的 303 份(8.4%)检测到 RSV,其中 5.9% 的 RSV 阳性成年人同时感染,主要是鼻病毒 (RV) 和流感病毒 (IFV)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究发现,RSV 合并感染以 RV 和 IFV 最为常见,并且根据高危情况,合并感染与单一感染之间没有统计学上的显着差异,这可能是由于统计功效有限。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,RSV 合并感染可能与高危成人疾病严重程度增加有关,这凸显了对该人群进行进一步研究和 监测 的必要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的样本量相对较小,检测到的 RSV 合并感染数量也较少,限制了检测合并感染和单一感染之间差异的能力。研究时期是在 COVID-19 大流行之前,不包括与 SARS-CoV-2 的合并感染。

title: Predictive modelling to differentiate possible bacterial and viral cases of childhood pneumonia in Kilifi, Kenya using protein markers and clinical data

source_records.title: Predictive modelling to differentiate possible bacterial and viral cases of childhood pneumonia in Kilifi, Kenya using protein markers and clinical data

priority_tier_reason: 高相关性，且具备高等级研究设计、全文证据或较强数据库/引用支持
full_text: BackgroundTo date, accessible diagnostic tools to identify whether a patient's pneumonia is a bacterial, or viral infection, are not accurate or timely enough to prevent preemptive antibiotic administration. Relying on single biomarkers or clinical presentations has been insufficient. We aimed to incorporate a wide range of novel biomarkers and clinical presentations into a multivariable model and to validate its ability to differentiate bacterial from viral pneumonia.MethodsA total of 457 children aged 2–59 months, admitted to the Kilifi County Referral Hospital, Kenya, with WHO defined pneumonia were classified using gold standard laboratory diagnostics as possible bacterial (i.e., bacterial/ unknown cases, n = 229) or possible viral (n = 228) infections. Clinical and laboratory data, and levels of CRP, PCT and 6 novel protein biomarkers were used to develop and validate a predictive multivariable Poisson regression model to differentiate pneumonia etiology. The Receiver Operating Characteristic curve was used to assess biomarker performance and validate the model internally.ResultsIn age-adjusted analyses, chest-wall indrawing, cough, convulsions, crackles, angiotensinogen (AGT), and Serpin Family A Member 1 (SERPINA1) were significantly associated with pneumonia etiology, controlling for age. However, only chest-wall indrawing remained significant in multivariable analyses after controlling for age. The model demonstrated fair, but inadequate, discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.61. In a separate analysis excluding the unknowns from the bacterial group, chest-wall indrawing, crackles, cough, AGT (>=7.9144MFI), were significant predictors of pneumonia etiology, adjusting for age. This model demonstrated good discrimination, with an Area Under the Curve of 0.78 on the validation dataset.ConclusionAmong children admitted to the hospital with WHO-defined pneumonia, modelling a wide range of biomarkers and clinical presentations still failed to distinguish bacterial from viral pneumonia with enough accuracy to guide clinical management. Further research addressing some of the limitations we encountered in outcome classification, stratifying by disease severity and potentially accounting for variation in biomarker performance by age, may improve predictions. Materials and methodsStudy setting and populationData on children presenting to Kilifi County Referral Hospital (KCRH) with pneumonia were derived from the long-term surveillance of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) in childhood lower respiratory tract infection study, conducted between January 2007 and August 2020. This project sampled children less than 5 years of age who were either febrile or presented with sepsis or pneumonia for biomarker discovery and validation (8). Children were excluded if born prematurely, were less than 1 week of age, or had a history of congenital heart disease. For the analysis presented here, this nested case-control study selected data from children aged 2–59 months who met the 2013 WHO definition of pneumonia (22). This study utilized secondary data, and therefore, the patients were participants in the study and were not involved in the design, conduct, or dissemination plan of this study's findings.Study proceduresUnder the surveillance protocol, anthropometric (e.g., weight, height), clinical (e.g., cough, cyanosis, hypoxemia), and demographic data (e.g., age, gender), blood samples, and nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal (NP/OP) swabs were collected at admission. NP/OP swabs were used to test for 15 common childhood viral infections, including adenovirus, parainfluenza virus (1,2,3, and 4), RSV (A and B), influenza (A, B, and C), rhinovirus, human metapneumovirus, and coronaviruses (OC43, NL63, and E229) using multiplex real-time PCR. Blood specimens were cultured for bacteria, and a blood slide was prepared to determine malaria infection status. Blood samples were analyzed with a complete blood count [WBC, red blood cell counts (RBC), platelets, neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils]. The biomarker discovery study tested the blood samples from a subset of children and quantified 418 plasma proteins using high-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS/MS) [11]. CRP and 6 other plasma proteins appeared predictive of infectious aetiology: angiotensinogen (AGT), Serpin Family A Member 1 (SERPINA1), Serpin Family A Member 3 (SERPINA3), Paraoxonase-1 (PON1), Histidine Rich Glycoprotein (HRG/B2R8I2), and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) [11] and were therefore considered for etiology differentiation for this study. Samples from the whole cohort of children were then tested for CRP, PCT, and these 6 novel proteins using the same mass spectrometry. The ILab Aries clinical biochemistry analyzer was used to measure a subset of 100 CRP samples, which were converted to concentrations (8). Laboratory sample testing was conducted at the KEMRI-Wellcome Trust Research Programme (KWTRP) in Kilifi, Kenya.Statistical analysesFor the secondary data analysis presented in this paper, pneumonia cases were classified as viral, bacterial, bacterial-viral co-infections, and unknown infections (Figure 1). For clinical relevance, we combined children with evidence of bacterial infections, bacterial-viral co-infections, and unknown infections into a single group (possible bacterial infections) that would need to receive empirical antibiotic therapy if presenting to a healthcare facility. Children whose NP/OP swabs were PCR + for viral infections known to cause pneumonia [adenovirus, parainfluenza virus (1,2,3, and 4), RSV (A and B), influenza (A, B, and C), and human metapneumovirus] were defined as the probable viral pneumonia group.Figure 1This is the participants’ flowchart. It provides a detailed explanation of the flow by which the study determined the working sample size. It also shows which criteria of participants were eliminated and the pathogens that guided our case definition.Flowchart illustrating sample selection for a study on severe acute infections in children, detailing initial enrollment, exclusion criteria, final classification into bacterial and viral groups, and splitting of the dataset into training and testing sets.Variables such as cough duration were missing in >25% of participants and excluded from the analysis. Using the training dataset, excluding children with infections of unknown aetiology and bacterial-viral co-infections, the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve was used to identify optimal cutoff points for the mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) values of biomarkers, enabling categorization into categorical variables with the highest sensitivity, specificity, and overall discriminatory ability. The cutpointr package in R was utilized to determine the optimal threshold of each biomarker using the Youden index (sensitivity + specificity – 1). To enhance the robustness of the estimates, a 5-fold cross-validation stratified by etiology was used to assess the discriminatory power of each candidate biomarker and to identify the optimal threshold (cut-offs). These derived cut-offs from the training set were then applied unchanged to the validation dataset. Further exploratory analyses to determine cut-off points for biomarkers were also identified by stratifying the dataset by age (<1 and ≥1 years, <2 and ≥2 years, and <3 and ≥3 years) on the entire dataset to assess whether cut-offs varied by age, as this has been reported in some previous literature (26). The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) was used to evaluate multicollinearity among variables. Highly correlated variables (VIF >2) were assessed for their discriminatory power. The variable with the lower AUC was dropped. Exploratory interaction analyses were conducted after the primary analyses to assess whether an interaction between pneumonia severity and the eight biomarkers, adjusting for age, could explain the biomarkers’ performance. Interaction terms were included in separate modified Poisson regression models and significance assessed using the Wald test with robust standard errors.Model developmentThe dataset was randomly split into two datasets, stratified by etiology; 70% of the data was used for training and 30% for model validation. Age was considered a priori as a confounder in every stage of the analysis. A modified Poisson regression model was used to assess the association between every predictor and the outcome. Covariates with a likelihood ratio test (LRT) p-value < 0.2 in the age-adjusted analyses were considered to improve model fit and were therefore included in the selection for the multivariable predictive model. The multivariable Poisson regression model was fitted using backward selection. Variables were iteratively removed from the multivariate model, and variables that significantly improved the model's fit (LRT p-value < 0.05) were retained in the final model. The overall sensitivity, specificity, and discriminative power (AUC) of the final model for distinguishing bacterial from viral pneumonia cases were assessed. To assess the stability of the model development process and performance, a 5-fold cross-validation, stratified by etiology, on the training set was performed. Within each fold, 4 folds were used as the model development sets, while one fold was held out for out-of-sample model validation. The complete model-building procedure was performed in each fold, adjusting for age. First, each predictor was assessed for its association with etiology, using an LRT p-value <0.2 to identify potential predictors for inclusion in the multivariable model. Backward elimination was then performed, and variables with an LRT p-value <0.05 were retained in the multivariable models. The models’ performance was then assessed on the out-of-sample validation dataset using the AUC. The overall model performance was recorded as the mean AUC of the 5 cross-validation folds.Model validationThe model's ability to distinguish between bacterial and viral pneumonia cases was assessed using Area Under the Curve (AUC) values on the validation dataset. Other published predictive models were also run on the validation dataset to determine comparative discriminatory power. An AUC of 0.5 indicated that the model cannot discriminate beyond chance; a value greater than 0.7 was considered moderate discrimination, while a value greater than 0.80 was regarded as good discrimination (23). The model's calibration was assessed using the calibration intercept, which measures how close the predicted risks are to the observed event (underestimation or overestimation), and the calibration slope, which indicates potential model overfit or underfit (23). We externally validated a previously published model (15), developed in a study of Indonesian children aged 2–59 months with pneumonia (WHO 2014 definition) who were hospitalised within 24 h of admission, by applying their logistic regression model to our dataset without modification. We defined the variables in their final model as in their publication, without refitting or recalibrating it. Another study (9) conducted in Western Australian children ≤17 years of age recommended a CRP cutoff of 72 mg/L in the presence of fever (≥38 °C) or absence of rhinorrhea. We validated these models using CRP data analysed on the ILab Aries clinical biochemistry analyser. All statistical analyses were conducted using R software version 4.5.1, and variable significance was evaluated at a 5% significance level.Ethics approvalThe long-term surveillance of RSV in childhood lower respiratory tract infections study (SSC 1055) was approved by the Kenya Medical Research Institute Scientific Ethics Research Unit (KEMRI–SERU) and conducted in accordance with the principles of Good Clinical Practice and Good Clinical Laboratory Practice (GCLP). Written informed consent was obtained from the participant's respective legal guardian or next of kin, and the study adhered to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. For this nested study, data were shared with the approval of the study Principal Investigator and the KWTRP data governance committee. ResultsAmong the 457 children enrolled in this study, 228 (49.9%) had NP/OP swabs PCR + for viral infections known to cause pneumonia and no evidence of other infections, 93 (20.4%) had a positive blood culture for a bacterial infection, 12 (2.6%) had a bacterial-viral co-infection, and 124 (27.1%) had unknown etiology (i.e., negative blood culture, negative PCR panel, negative malaria slide; Figure 1). Among the 228 with a viral infection, the most identified viral pathogens were RSV-A (n = 39, 17.1%), parainfluenza-3 (n = 36, 15.8%), human metapneumovirus (n = 35, 15.4%), influenza-A (n = 34, 14.9%), and adenovirus (n = 28, 12.3%). The most identified bacterial pathogens from blood cultures were Escherichia coli (n = 17, 7.4%), Streptococcus pneumoniae (n = 17, 7.4%), Staphylococcus aureus (n = 11, 4.8%), and Haemophilus influenzae (n = 8, 3.5%).
